name: Isidorus of Aegae
bio: Isidorus of Aegae is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Wreath of Philippus, the Garland compiled in the first century AD.
This archive carries the 4 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 156, 280, 293, 532).

poems.title: Book VII, 156
poems.author: Isidorus of Aegae
poems.text: By his bird-lime and canes Eumelus lived on the creatures of the air, simply but in freedom. Never did he kiss a strange hand for his belly’s sake. This his craft supplied him with luxury and delight. Ninety years he lived, and now sleeps here, having left to his children his bird-lime, nets and canes.

poems.title: Book VII, 280
poems.author: Isidorus of Aegae
poems.text: This hummock is a tomb; you there hold in your oxen and pull up the ploughshare, for you are disturbing ashes. On such earth shed no seed of corn, but tears.

poems.title: Book VII, 293
poems.author: Isidorus of Aegae
poems.text: No tempest, no stormy setting of a constellation overwhelmed Nicophemus in the waters of the Libyan Sea. But alas, unhappy man stayed by a calm he was burnt up by thirst. This too was the work of the winds. Ah, what a curse are they to sailors, whether they blow or be silent!

poems.title: Book VII, 532
poems.author: Isidorus of Aegae
poems.text: I am Eteocles whom the hopes of the sea drew from husbandry and made a merchant in place of what I was by nature. I was travelling on the surface of the Tyrrhenian Sea, but with my ship I sunk headlong into its depths in a sudden fierce squall. It is not then the same wind that blows on the threshing-floor and fills the sails.
